title: My Two Books of Preludes and Fugues Have Been Released!
content_blocks: My two books of Preludes and Fugues for Solo Piano have been released, on a double album from Bridge Records! David Starobin, President of Bridge, has had some very kind things to say about it (one excerpt: “Every once in a while a project comes by which seems so original that I am challenged to re-screw my ears on. Such was the case with David S. Lefkowitz's nearly three-hour long cycle of Preludes and Fugues for Piano.” More here, and here), as have several other musicians and colleagues. In this post I wanted to introduce how they came about. I’ll describe what the two books are all about subsequently, and talk about individual prelude and fugues later.

The 7-century history of fugue reached a peak in the 18th century with J.S. Bach’s two-volume Well-Tempered Clavier and the Art of the Fugue. The Well-Tempered Clavier established the template of prelude introducing the key and fugue exploring it—covering all keys from C major through B minor. Other composers have written similar sets of preludes and fugues, including Mendelssohn, 20th-century American composers Hindemith and Diamond, and Russian composers Shostakovich, Slonimsky, and Kapustin.

I started writing these two sets of preludes and fugues right at the beginning of Covid in spring 2020, for a UCLA Music Department’s Division of Composition project headed by Richard Danielpour and featuring Stefano Greco. Having written one pair, I decided to write another. This led to a set of ten, starting and ending in C, but leaving D-flat, E-flat, and A-flat out. In the midst of the pandemic, I put together videos of those ten preludes and fugues, which I called “18 from ’20: Preludes and Fugues by David S. Lefkowitz” (two of the ten pressed the prelude and the fugue together—blurring the lines between them—so that the ten pairs were actually only eighteen separate pieces) and posted those to YouTube. With each new pair I felt more and more like I had found where I needed to be compositionally, so I expanded that set of ten to thirteen (adding the ones in D-flat, E-flat, and A-flat), creating Expanded Universe: 13 Preludes and Fugues for Solo Piano, completed in September 2021.

Well, if one book of preludes and fugues is good, why not two? After all, Bach did it! So, while adding the finishing touches for the first book, I embarked on a second book, which I finished in September, 2022. This book is written for prepared piano, changing the sound of the instrument completely, and generating completely different “worlds” of music, creating Parallel Universes: 13 Preludes and Fugues for Solo Pianos and Piano Duo.

The next step was to go into the recording studio.  I first enlisted the help of David Kaplan, a friend and colleague at UCLA, to anchor the project.  We agreed to divide the nearly three hours of music (!) between four pianists:  Steve Beck, Michael Mizrahi, Mika Sasaki, and David Kaplan.  I helped out with an additional piano bass line, a special in-the-piano technique, and with some whistling, and Cantor Marcus Feldman sang a vocal part as well.  Post-production took almost a year and a half, but at last, in Summer, 2024, it was ready to send off.  David Starobin agreed to release it on Bridge, and now—some three months more than five years after I first started composition—it has been released.  There is truly something for everybody here, so please sample different tracks—I hope that you enjoy the music!
Here is a YouTube playlist with all of the pieces. In my next two posts I’ll explain what a fugue is and how my approach is new. I’ll provide links to individual pieces in the later posts.

“Every once in a while a project comes by which seems so original that I am challenged to re-screw my ears on. Such was the case with David S. Lefkowitz's nearly three-hour long cycle of Preludes and Fugues for Piano.”
